questiontext.text: What is a struct used for?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A struct gathers related data under one name, so a student's name and score can travel together as a single object.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Grouping variables of different types into one new type

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Point {
    int x;
    int y;
};

int main() {
    Point a = {1, 2};
    Point b = a;
    b.x = 7;
    cout << a.x << " " << b.x << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Point b = a; makes an independent copy. Changing b.x does not touch a, so a.x stays 1 while b.x is 7.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

int main() {

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Braces fill the members in order, and every member that is not mentioned is zeroed. So x is 7 and y is 0.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Counter {
    int hits;
};

void a(Counter c) {
    c.hits += 5;
}

void b(Counter& c) {
    c.hits += 2;
}

int main() {
    Counter k{1};
    a(k);
    b(k);
    cout << k.hits << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Function a receives a copy, so its +5 is lost. Function b receives a reference, so its +2 changes the original: 1 + 2 = 3.

questiontext.text:
Arrange the steps for finding the best student in a vector.

Drag the steps into the correct order.

1. [[1]]

2. [[2]]

3. [[3]]

4. [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The type has to exist before a vector can hold it. We need a starting value for best before the loop can compare against it, and the answer is printed only after the loop has seen every student.

The correct answer:

  1. Define the struct Student
  2. Read the students into a vector
  3. Start with best equal to the first student
  4. Loop over the students and replace best when a score is higher

questiontext.text:
Match each term with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Struct  →  [[1]]

Member  →  [[2]]

Object  →  [[3]]

Member function  →  [[4]]

Dot  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These five words describe how a struct is built and used: the type, its members, the objects made from it, the functions inside it, and the dot that reaches them.

The correct answer:

  • Struct → A new type that groups several members
  • Member → A variable or function inside the struct
  • Object → A variable made from the struct type
  • Member function → A function defined inside the struct
  • Dot → The symbol that reaches a member, as in p.x

questiontext.text:
Sort each statement: does it compile? (struct Point { int x; int y; }; Point p = {1, 2}; is declared above)

Drag the correct label next to every item.

cout << p.x;  →  [[1]]

cout << p.z;  →  [[2]]

p.y = 5;  →  [[1]]

cout << p;  →  [[2]]

Point q = p;  →  [[1]]

p.x();  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Members are reached by name, so a missing member is an error. A whole struct cannot be printed with <<, so we print its members one by one, and x is a number, not a function. These statements were all tested with a real compiler.

The correct answer:

Compiles: cout << p.x;, p.y = 5;, Point q = p;
Does not compile: cout << p.z;, cout << p;, p.x();

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

struct Item {
    string name;
    int price;
};

int main() {
    vector<Item> v = {{"pen", 3}, {"ink", 1}, {"cap", 3}};
    int sum = 0;
    for (const Item& it : v) {
        if (it.price >= 3) {
            sum += it.price;
        }
    }
    cout << sum << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Only the items with price 3 or more are added: pen (3) and cap (3). The ink costs 1, so it is skipped. The sum is 3 + 3 = 6.

questiontext.text: Which parameter type lets a function read a big struct without copying it and without changing it?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. const forbids changes and & avoids the copy. A plain Student copies the whole object, and Student& allows changes.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Rect {
    int w;
    int h;
    int area() const {
        return w * h;
    }
};

int main() {
    Rect r = {4, 6};
    Rect q = r;
    q.w = 5;
    cout << r.area() << " " << q.area() << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. q is a copy of r, so changing q.w to 5 does not affect r. The area of r stays 4 x 6 = 24, while the area of q is 5 x 6 = 30.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Rect {
    int w;
    int h;
    int area() const { return w * h; }
    int perimeter() const { return 2 * (w + h); }
};

int main() {
    Rect r = {3, 4};
    cout << r.area() << " " << r.perimeter() << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The braces store w = 3 and h = 4. The area is 3 x 4 = 12, and the perimeter is 2 x (3 + 4) = 14, so the program prints 12 14.

name.text: Q14 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct operator into the gap so the program prints the name of the student with the highest score (Bo).

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

struct S {
    string name;
    int score;
};

int main() {
    vector<S> v = {{"Al", 3}, {"Bo", 9}, {"Cy", 5}};
    S best = v[0];
    for (const S& s : v) {
        if (s.score [[1]] best.score) {
            best = s;
        }
    }
    cout << best.name << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. We replace best whenever a student has a higher score, so > is needed. With < or == nobody ever replaces Al, and the program would print Al.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

struct S {
    string name;
    int score;
};

int main() {
    vector<S> v = {{"Al", 3}, {"Bo", 9}, {"Cy", 5}};
    S best = v[0];
    for (const S& s : v) {
        if (s.score > best.score) {
            best = s;
        }
    }
    cout << best.name << endl;
    return 0;
}

questiontext.text:
Match each declaration with what it means.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Point q = p;  →  [[1]]

Point& q = p;  →  [[2]]

const Point& q = p;  →  [[3]]

p.x  →  [[4]]

Point p{};  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The ampersand decides whether we copy or alias, and const decides whether we may change.

The correct answer:

  • Point q = p; → An independent copy of p
  • Point& q = p; → Another name for p itself
  • const Point& q = p; → A read-only alias, no copy
  • p.x → The member x of the object p
  • Point p{}; → An object with every member zeroed

Arrange the lines so the program prints 92 50.

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The type must be declared first, then s is created, then copied into t. Only then do we change t, and we print last. Because t is an independent copy, s keeps 92.

The correct answer:

questiontext.text:
Sort each function: is the parameter passed by value (a copy) or by reference?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

void f(Point p)  →  [[1]]

void f(Point& p)  →  [[2]]

void f(const Point& p)  →  [[2]]

void f(Point q, int k)  →  [[1]]

int g(const Student& s)  →  [[2]]

void h(Student s)  →  [[1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. No ampersand means the function receives a copy. An ampersand, with or without const, means it works on the original object.

The correct answer:

By value (copy): void f(Point p), void f(Point q, int k), void h(Student s)
By reference: void f(Point& p), void f(const Point& p), int g(const Student& s)

questiontext.text: When is a struct a better choice than a pair?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A pair gives only first and second. A struct lets you write name and score, and it can hold as many members as you need.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: When you want meaningful member names or more than two members
When you need the fastest possible code
When you want a container that is always sorted
When you want to avoid headers

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

struct S {
    string name;
    int score;
};

int main() {
    vector<S> v = {{"A", 3}, {"B", 9}, {"C", 9}};
    S best = v[0];
    for (const S& s : v) {
        if (s.score > best.score) {
            best = s;
        }
    }
    cout << best.name << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The loop replaces best only when a score is strictly greater. B (9) beats A (3), but C (9) is not greater than 9, so B stays.
